callouts.p: Always state that dry mass is used because water content in living organisms varies constantly. Always use the phrase 'dried until constant mass is reached'.

core.h: Pyramids of Biomass vs Pyramids of Number
core.p: Pyramids of biomass display the total dry mass at each trophic level, whereas pyramids of number simply display the total count of individual organisms regardless of their size.
bullets: **Pyramids of Number** can have an inverted shape (e.g. a single large oak tree supporting thousands of insects).
**Pyramids of Biomass** are almost always pyramid-shaped (broadest at the bottom and narrowing towards the top) because biomass is lost at each transfer.

Exceptions to biomass pyramids occur rarely in aquatic ecosystems (e.g. phytoplankton reproducing extremely rapidly to support a larger mass of zooplankton), but for GCSE OCR J247, terrestrial pyramids of biomass are strictly upright.

callouts.p: Never draw a pyramid of biomass with an inverted base unless specifically instructed by atypical marine phytoplankton data. Standard terrestrial biomass pyramids always narrow at every higher level.

core.h: Rules for Constructing Pyramids of Biomass
core.p: Constructing an accurate pyramid of biomass requires following precise graphical conventions specified by OCR mark schemes.
bullets: **Positioning**: Producers (Trophic Level 1) must always be at the very bottom bar.
**Bar Alignment**: The bars must be drawn horizontally and centered symmetrically along a vertical axis.
**Scale**: The width of each bar must be strictly proportional to the quantity of biomass at that trophic level.
**Height**: The vertical height of every bar in the pyramid must be identical.
**Labelling**: Each bar must be clearly labelled with the organism name or its trophic level, including correct units (e.g., g/m²).

core.h: Pathways of Biomass Loss: Uneaten Material
core.p: Not all available biomass at one trophic level is consumed by the organism at the next trophic level.
bullets: Predators rarely eat every single component of their prey.
**Indigestible or inaccessible structures** are left behind, such as bones, teeth, claws, horns, fur, and feathers in animals.
In plants, roots, woody stems, coarse bark, and fallen leaves are often left unconsumed by herbivores.
This unconsumed biomass enters the decomposer pathway (detritivores and decomposers) rather than passing to the next consumer level.

core.p: Biomass that is ingested by a consumer is not entirely absorbed into the consumer's bloodstream and tissues.
bullets: **Egestion** is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed waste material from the digestive tract as faeces.
Herbivores ingest large amounts of **cellulose** from plant cell walls, which many animals lack the cellulase enzymes to digest.
Because this cellulose cannot be digested or absorbed across the intestinal wall, it passes straight through the gut and is egested.
Egested material contains organic chemical energy and biomass that is lost from the main consumer food chain.

callouts.p: The discharge or expulsion of undigested material (faeces) from the digestive tract. This is material that was ingested but never absorbed into cells.

core.p: Excretion involves removing the metabolic waste products produced inside cells from metabolic reactions.
bullets: **Excretion** differs fundamentally from egestion: excreted material was absorbed and metabolized within body cells.
Excess proteins and amino acids are broken down in the liver (deamination) to form **urea**, which is excreted in urine.
Excreted molecules represent lost nitrogenous biomass compounds that cannot be used to build consumer tissue.
Water lost in excretion is part of metabolic waste, though biomass calculations focus on the dry organic mass of molecules like urea.

callouts.p: Examiners frequently test the difference. Egestion is undigested food leaving the anus (faeces). Excretion is waste from cellular metabolism leaving via kidneys/lungs (urine/CO2).

core.h: Pathways of Biomass Loss: Respiration and Heat
core.p: Respiration is the primary metabolic driver of biomass loss in consumers and producers alike.
bullets: Absorbed glucose and organic nutrient molecules are oxidized during **aerobic cellular respiration** to produce ATP for biological work.
Equation: Glucose + Oxygen -> Carbon Dioxide + Water.
The carbon atoms in glucose are converted into **carbon dioxide gas (CO₂)** and released into the atmosphere via gas exchange, directly reducing the physical mass of the organism.
Respiration drives essential life processes: muscle contraction (movement), active transport, protein synthesis, and cell division.
Respiration is an exothermic reaction; energy is lost to the surroundings as **thermal energy (heat)**, which cannot be converted back into biological biomass.

callouts.p: Carbon dioxide gas (CO₂) released during cellular respiration is the main molecule responsible for the loss of dry mass from an organism's body.

core.p: The efficiency of biomass transfer measures the percentage of biomass at one trophic level that is successfully converted into new biomass at the next trophic level.
bullets: **Standard Transfer Formula**:
$$\text{Efficiency of biomass transfer (\%)} = \left( \frac{\text{Biomass incorporated into next trophic level}}{\text{Biomass available at previous trophic level}} \right) \times 100$$
Typically, only about **10%** of biomass is transferred successfully between trophic levels in natural ecosystems (ranging between 5% and 20%).
**Percentage Loss Formula**:
$$\text{Percentage Loss (\%)} = \left( \frac{\text{Biomass lost}}{\text{Biomass available at lower level}} \right) \times 100 = 100\% - \text{Efficiency (\%)}$$

core.h: Why Efficiency Limits Food Chain Length
core.p: Because ~90% of biomass is lost at each successive step in a food chain, higher trophic levels receive exponentially smaller amounts of biomass and energy.
bullets: By trophic level 4 or 5, the total biomass available is insufficient to support a viable population of apex predators.
Apex predators must spend excessive energy hunting across vast territories to consume enough biomass to meet their basic metabolic demands.
Consequently, food chains rarely contain more than **4 or 5 trophic levels**.

core.h: Endotherms versus Ectotherms: Impact on Transfer Efficiency
core.p: The physiological group to which an animal belongs significantly impacts its biomass transfer efficiency.
bullets: **Endotherms** (mammals and birds) maintain a constant internal body temperature using heat released from metabolic respiration.
Endotherms have a **lower biomass transfer efficiency** (often 1-3%) because they respire at a high rate to generate thermal energy.
**Ectotherms** (fish, reptiles, amphibians, invertebrates) rely on external heat sources to warm their bodies.
Ectotherms lose far less biomass through respiration, yielding a **higher biomass transfer efficiency** (often 10-20%) as more absorbed biomass is allocated to growth.

core.h: Practical Context: Determining Dry Biomass Experimentally
core.p: OCR practical skills (PAG contexts) require students to know how dry mass of biological samples is determined accurately.
bullets: 1. Collect a representative sample of organisms from the designated area.
2. Record the initial wet mass using an electronic balance.
3. Place the sample in a drying oven set to a low temperature (approx. 80°C) to evaporate water without combusting organic matter.
4. Periodically remove the sample, cool it in a desiccator, and record its mass on a balance.
5. Repeat the heating and weighing steps until the mass remains identical on two consecutive weighings (**constant mass**).
6. Record this value as the final **dry biomass**.

callouts.p: Do not set ovens above 100°C because excessive heat burns organic tissue (turning biomass into smoke/ash), causing an overestimation of lost biological material.

analogy.p: Think of biomass transfer as a salary pipeline passing down generations. Out of $100 earned by a parent (Producer biomass), $90 is immediately spent on essential living bills like rent/heating (Respiration loss as heat/CO2), unusable junk purchases thrown in the trash (Egestion/Faeces), and taxes (Excretion/Urine), leaving only $10 to put into a savings account (New biomass growth). The child (Primary consumer) can only inherit that $10 savings account. When the child receives it, they too must spend 90% of it on their own bills, leaving only $1 for the grandchild (Secondary consumer). Where the analogy breaks down: Monetary currency can recycled endlessly in a circular economy, whereas energy/biomass lost as respiratory heat to space cannot be re-absorbed by green plants.

mistakes.w: Egestion and excretion mean the exact same thing.
mistakes.r: Egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces via the anus. Excretion is the removal of metabolic cellular waste products such as urea in urine or CO2 from lungs.

mistakes.w: Energy and biomass are destroyed during respiration.
mistakes.r: Biomass is converted into chemical waste products (CO2 gas and H2O) and energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat; matter and energy are conserved, not destroyed.

mistakes.w: Pyramids of biomass can be inverted just like pyramids of numbers.
mistakes.r: Terrestrial pyramids of biomass are almost always upright because biomass decreases at each progressive trophic level due to cumulative transfer losses.

mistakes.w: Wet mass is more accurate because drying kills organisms.
mistakes.r: Dry mass is far more accurate because wet mass varies constantly with hydration, weather, and water intake.

mistakes.w: Sunlight falling on soil is a loss of biomass between trophic levels.
mistakes.r: Unabsorbed sunlight is inefficient light capture by producers, not a biomass loss between biological trophic levels.

mistakes.w: Plants do not lose biomass through respiration.
mistakes.r: Plants undergo aerobic respiration 24 hours a day, breaking down glucose into carbon dioxide gas, which reduces dry biomass.

mistakes.w: Drawing pyramid bars with different vertical heights.
mistakes.r: All horizontal bars in a drawn pyramid of biomass must have equal vertical height; only their horizontal width varies to show scale.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply by 100 when calculating biomass transfer efficiency percentage.
mistakes.r: Always multiply the decimal fraction (Biomass output / Biomass input) by 100 to present the answer as a percentage.

exam.q: Define the term biomass. [1 mark]
model: The total dry mass of living biological material in an organism or specified area.
exam.tip: Include the word 'dry' to secure the full mark.

exam.q: Explain why measuring dry mass is preferred over wet mass when determining the biomass of organisms in an ecosystem. [2 marks]
model: Water content in living organisms varies constantly / fluctuates significantly.
Dry mass provides an accurate, reliable measure of actual organic cellular material.
exam.tip: Focus your answer on water fluctuation vs true biological tissue.

exam.q: Describe how a scientist would accurately determine the dry biomass of a plant sample. [3 marks]
model: Weigh the plant sample and place it in an oven at a low temperature (e.g. 80°C).
Re-weigh the sample at regular intervals.
Continue drying until two consecutive mass measurements are identical (constant mass is reached).
exam.tip: Mentioning 'constant mass' and 'low temperature' are key mark scheme keywords.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why not all biomass ingested by a primary consumer is converted into new biomass in its body. [2 marks]
model: Some eaten material cannot be digested (e.g. cellulose) and is lost as egested faeces.
Biomass is broken down in respiration to release energy, releasing carbon dioxide gas and water.
exam.tip: Make sure to state egestion/faeces or respiration/CO2 clearly.

exam.q: Distinguish clearly between the processes of egestion and excretion. [2 marks]
model: Egestion is the removal of undigested/unabsorbed food material as faeces from the gut.
Excretion is the removal of waste products produced by metabolic reactions inside cells (e.g. urea, CO2).
exam.tip: Emphasize cellular metabolic origin for excretion vs gut passage for egestion.

exam.q: A meadow contains 8000 g/m² of grass. Herbivores consume this grass and synthesize 880 g/m² of primary consumer biomass. Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer between producers and primary consumers. [2 marks]
model: Calculation: (880 / 8000) * 100
Answer: 11%
exam.tip: Show working out clearly: (Output / Input) x 100.

exam.q: Explain why food chains rarely contain more than four or five trophic levels. [3 marks]
model: Biomass/energy is lost at every trophic level (via respiration, faeces, uneaten parts).
Only about 10% of biomass is transferred to the next level.
At higher levels, insufficient biomass/energy remains to support a viable population of apex predators.
exam.tip: Connect the ~90% cumulative loss to the inability to sustain top predator populations.

exam.q: Explain why a mammal has a lower biomass transfer efficiency than a cold-blooded fish of similar size. [3 marks]
model: Mammals are endotherms that maintain a constant internal body temperature.
They have higher rates of cellular respiration to generate metabolic heat energy.
More biomass (glucose) is oxidized to CO2 gas and lost, leaving less biomass available for growth/tissue.
exam.tip: Link endothermy -> higher respiration -> lost CO2/heat -> lower growth efficiency.

exam.q: State the trophic level occupied by a snake that eats herbivorous field mice. [1 mark]
model: Trophic Level 3 (Secondary Consumer).
exam.tip: Grass (1) -> Mouse (2) -> Snake (3).

exam.q: Explain how biomass is lost from a food chain through the process of cellular respiration. [6 marks]
model: Organisms absorb organic molecules such as glucose during digestion.
Cells break down glucose in aerobic respiration using oxygen.
Respiration releases chemical energy (ATP) required for cellular processes such as active transport and muscle contraction.
Carbon atoms in glucose are combined with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide (CO2).
Carbon dioxide is a gas that is exhaled/released into the surrounding atmosphere, directly removing mass from the organism.
Respiration is an exothermic process, transferring energy to the surroundings as heat which cannot be recaptured as biomass.
exam.tip: Structure logically: absorption -> cellular breakdown -> CO2 gas exhaled (mass loss) -> thermal energy loss.

worked.q:
An ecosystem data table shows the dry biomass at four trophic levels:
- Producers: 12,000 g/m²
- Primary Consumers: 1,320 g/m²
- Secondary Consumers: 105.6 g/m²
- Tertiary Consumers: 8.45 g/m²

a) Calculate the percentage efficiency of biomass transfer from Primary Consumers to Secondary Consumers.
b) Calculate the total percentage of producer biomass that reaches the Tertiary Consumer level.
steps: Step 1 (Part a): Identify the biomass input (Primary Consumers = 1,320 g/m²) and output (Secondary Consumers = 105.6 g/m²).
Step 2 (Part a): Use efficiency formula: (Output / Input) * 100 = (105.6 / 1320) * 100.
Step 4 (Part b): Identify initial producer biomass (12,000 g/m²) and final tertiary consumer biomass (8.45 g/m²).
Step 5 (Part b): Calculate overall efficiency: (8.45 / 12000) * 100 = 0.00070416 * 100 = 0.0704%.
worked.ans:
a) Efficiency from Primary to Secondary Consumer = 8.0%
b) Percentage of Producer biomass reaching Tertiary Consumer = 0.0704% (or 0.07%)

worked.q:
A student dries a 250.0 g fresh sample of clover plant in an oven at 80°C to determine its dry mass. The mass recorded over consecutive hours is:
- Hour 0: 250.0 g
- Hour 2: 140.0 g
- Hour 4: 65.0 g
- Hour 6: 42.5 g
- Hour 8: 42.5 g

a) State the final dry biomass of the sample and justify your answer.
b) Calculate the percentage water content of the original fresh clover sample.
steps: Step 1 (Part a): Look for identical consecutive readings. Hour 6 = 42.5 g and Hour 8 = 42.5 g.
Step 2 (Part a): The mass remains constant at 42.5 g, indicating all water has evaporated.
Step 3 (Part b): Calculate water mass lost = Fresh mass - Dry mass = 250.0 g - 42.5 g = 207.5 g.
Step 4 (Part b): Calculate percentage water content = (Mass of water lost / Fresh mass) * 100 = (207.5 / 250.0) * 100 = 83.0%.
worked.ans:
a) Dry biomass = 42.5 g because the mass remained constant between Hours 6 and 8.
b) Water content = 83.0%

bio_ocra.10.5.summary: Interdependence and competition describe how species interact within ecosystems. **Predation**, **mutualism** and **parasitism** are three key relationships that drive energy flow, nutrient cycling and population control. Understanding the mechanisms, benefits and costs of each interaction helps explain community structure and the stability of ecosystems.

core.p: Clear, exam‑ready definitions are essential for full marks.
bullets: Predation – a **biotic interaction** where one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey).
Mutualism – a **symbiotic relationship** in which **both** species benefit.
Parasitism – a **symbiotic relationship** where the **parasite** benefits at the **expense** of the host, usually without killing it.

callouts.p: The predator obtains energy and nutrients by killing and consuming the prey.
Both organisms gain a fitness advantage that enhances survival or reproduction.
The parasite derives nutrients from the host, which may suffer reduced growth, reproduction or increased mortality.

core.p: Predators use adaptations to locate, capture and subdue prey; prey evolve counter‑adaptations, creating an evolutionary ‘arms race’.
bullets: Adaptations of predators: sharp teeth/claws, keen senses, speed, camouflage, venom.
Adaptations of prey: camouflage, warning colours, speed, defensive structures (spines, shells), grouping behaviour.
Result: regulates prey populations, influences community composition and drives natural selection.

callouts.p: Predation prevents any one species from dominating, maintaining biodiversity.

core.p: Mutualistic relationships can be **obligate** (both species cannot survive without each other) or **facultative** (they can survive alone but benefit when together).
bullets: Pollination – insects (e.g., bees) obtain nectar; plants receive pollen transfer.
Mycorrhizal fungi – fungi increase water/mineral uptake for plants; plants supply carbohydrates.
Gut flora – bacteria aid digestion in animals; bacteria receive a protected environment and nutrients.

callouts.p: Both partners often evolve traits that enhance the mutualism (e.g., flower shape matching pollinator mouthparts).

core.p: Parasites obtain resources from a host, often causing disease or reduced fitness, but usually do not kill the host outright because they rely on it for continued nourishment.
bullets: Types: endoparasites (inside host – e.g., tapeworms) and ectoparasites (on surface – e.g., ticks).
Transmission routes: direct contact, vectors, ingestion of eggs/cysts.
Host response: immune defence, behavioural changes (grooming), sometimes tolerance.

callouts.p: Do not describe parasitism as ‘mutualism with one side harmed’; it is a distinct category in the mark scheme.

core.p: Predation directly transfers energy from prey to predator; mutualism and parasitism also involve energy/nutrient exchange but differ in net gain/loss for the participants.
bullets: Predation: 10 % of the prey’s energy is assimilated by the predator (energy transfer efficiency).
Mutualism: both partners gain energy or nutrients; the net gain for the community is positive.
Parasitism: parasite gains energy at the host’s expense; overall community efficiency may be reduced.

callouts.p: Only about 10 % of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next – applies to predation.

core.p: Classic Lotka‑Volterra cycles illustrate how predator and prey numbers rise and fall in a regular pattern.
bullets: When prey are abundant, predator numbers increase (more food).
As predators increase, prey numbers decline (more being eaten).
Fewer prey cause predator numbers to fall, allowing prey to recover – cycle repeats.

callouts.p: Sketch a simple sine‑wave style graph with prey leading predator by one quarter cycle – a common exam mark.

core.p: When two species interact closely, natural selection can act on both, leading to reciprocal adaptations.
bullets: Predator‑prey: faster prey ↔ faster predators.
Mutualism: flower colour & shape ↔ pollinator tongue length.
Parasitism: host immune defences ↔ parasite evasion strategies.

callouts.p: A continual cycle of adaptation and counter‑adaptation.

core.p: Human activities can disrupt these relationships, leading to ecosystem imbalance.
bullets: Over‑hunting removes top predators → prey overpopulation → habitat degradation.
Pesticides kill pollinators → reduced plant reproduction.
Introduced parasites (e.g., *Varroa* mite) can decimate native species.

callouts.p: Never state that all parasites are ‘bad’ for ecosystems; some regulate host populations.

core.p: Typical practical investigations used in OCR assessments.
bullets: Predation rate: place a known number of prey (e.g., fruit flies) with a predator (e.g., spiders) and count survivors after a set time.
Mutualism benefit: compare seed set of plants with and without pollinator access (bagged vs. open flowers).
Parasitism impact: measure growth rate of infected vs. uninfected host organisms.

callouts.p: Use bar charts; label axes clearly – a common mark‑scheme requirement.

core.p: Predation, mutualism and parasitism are three fundamental ways organisms interact, each influencing energy flow, population size and evolutionary trajectories.
bullets: **Predation** – kills, controls numbers, drives adaptations.
**Mutualism** – reciprocal benefit, can be obligate or facultative, promotes co‑evolution.
**Parasitism** – one benefits, the other is harmed but usually not killed, can regulate host populations.

analogy.t: The ecosystem as a bustling marketplace
analogy.p: Imagine an ecosystem like a market. Predators are the shop owners who buy (eat) goods (prey) from stalls, keeping the market from being over‑stocked. Mutualists are two stall owners who agree to trade – one sells honey, the other sells pollen, each gaining more customers. Parasites are like a pickpocket who takes money from a shopper without the shopper’s consent but doesn’t push them out of the market. The analogy breaks down because, unlike a market, energy cannot be created – it must flow from producers up the food chain, and the ‘pickpocket’ can sometimes cause the shopper to leave permanently, which is rare for most parasites.

terms.d: An organism that hunts, kills and eats another organism (prey).
An organism that is hunted and eaten by a predator.
A symbiotic relationship where both species benefit.
A mutualistic relationship in which each species cannot survive without the other.
A mutualistic relationship where each species can survive alone but gains an advantage when together.
A symbiotic relationship where the parasite benefits at the host’s expense, usually without killing the host.
A parasite that lives inside the host’s body (e.g., tapeworm).
A parasite that lives on the surface of the host (e.g., tick).
Reciprocal evolutionary change in two interacting species.
A cycle of adaptations and counter‑adaptations between interacting species.
A mathematical description of predator‑prey population cycles.
Only about 10 % of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next.
A close, long‑term interaction between two different species.
A step in a food chain or food web (producer, primary consumer, etc.).
A living component of an ecosystem that influences other organisms.

mistakes.w: Parasitism is the same as mutualism but with one side harmed
mistakes.r: Parasitism is a distinct type of symbiosis where only the parasite benefits; mutualism benefits both parties.

mistakes.w: Predators always kill their prey instantly
mistakes.r: Predators may kill quickly or use venom/slow consumption; the key is that the prey is killed and eaten.

mistakes.w: All mutualisms are obligate
mistakes.r: Many mutualisms are facultative; the species can survive alone but have increased fitness together.

mistakes.w: Parasites always kill their hosts
mistakes.r: Parasites usually do not kill the host because they rely on it for resources.

mistakes.w: Energy is transferred at 100 % efficiency in predation
mistakes.r: Only about 10 % of the energy is transferred to the next trophic level.

mistakes.w: Predation only affects prey numbers, not predator numbers
mistakes.r: Predator numbers are directly linked to prey availability; both populations fluctuate together.

mistakes.w: Mutualism cannot involve animals
mistakes.r: Animal‑animal mutualisms exist (e.g., cleaning symbiosis between fish).

mistakes.w: Parasites are always larger than their hosts
mistakes.r: Parasites are often much smaller (e.g., tapeworms in mammals).

mistakes.w: If a species is a predator it cannot be a prey at another life stage
mistakes.r: Many organisms are both predators and prey at different life stages (e.g., frogs).

mistakes.w: All competition is interspecific
mistakes.r: Competition can be intraspecific (within the same species) as well as interspecific.

exam.q: Define predation and give one example relevant to a UK ecosystem.
model: Predation is a biotic interaction where one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey).
Example: red fox preying on field vole.
exam.tip: Use the exact wording ‘kills and eats’ – examiners look for this phrase.

exam.q: Explain how mutualism can be obligate, using the relationship between mycorrhizal fungi and plants.
model: Mycorrhizal fungi increase the surface area of plant roots, improving water and mineral uptake (benefit to plant).
In return the plant supplies the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis (benefit to fungi).
Both partners are unable to survive long‑term without the other, making the relationship obligate.
exam.tip: State the two-way benefit and then link to ‘obligate’ definition.

exam.q: Describe two adaptations of predators and two adaptations of prey that illustrate an evolutionary arms race.
model: Predator adaptations: (1) Sharp teeth/claws for killing, (2) Acute vision for locating prey.
Prey adaptations: (1) Camouflage colouration to avoid detection, (2) Speed or warning colours to deter attack.
exam.tip: Link each adaptation back to the concept of an arms race.

exam.q: A population of rabbits is introduced to an island with no natural predators. Predict what will happen to the rabbit population over time and explain why.
model: Initially the rabbit population will increase rapidly because there is abundant food and no predation pressure.
Eventually resources become limited, leading to competition, disease and a possible crash in numbers (logistic growth).
exam.tip: Mention both the lack of predation and the later limiting factors.

exam.q: Explain the difference between mutualism and parasitism, giving one example of each.
model: Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship where both species benefit (e.g., bee and flower).
Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship where one species benefits at the expense of the other (e.g., tick on a dog).
exam.tip: Use the exact terms ‘both benefit’ and ‘one benefits, the other is harmed’.

exam.q: Using a diagram, illustrate a simple predator‑prey cycle and label the phases.
model: Diagram showing sinusoidal curves for prey (leading) and predator (lagging).
Labels: increase in prey, increase in predators, decrease in prey, decrease in predators.
exam.tip: Make sure the predator curve lags behind the prey by a quarter cycle – a common marking point.

exam.q: Discuss how the removal of a top predator can affect a mutualistic relationship in the same ecosystem.
model: Removal of top predator can cause prey (e.g., herbivores) to increase, leading to over‑grazing of plants that host pollinators. This reduces flower abundance, weakening pollination mutualism. Additionally, increased herbivore numbers may spread parasites that affect pollinators, further disrupting the mutualism. The cascade shows indirect effects of predator loss on other interactions.
exam.tip: Structure answer: (1) direct effect of predator loss, (2) indirect effect on plant‑pollinator mutualism, (3) link to ecosystem stability.

exam.q: State two ways in which parasites can regulate host populations and give an example for each.
model: Parasites can reduce host reproductive output (e.g., *Plasmodium* reduces bird breeding success).
Parasites can increase host mortality (e.g., *Varroa* mite causing colony collapse in honeybees).
exam.tip: Focus on ‘regulate’ – mention reduced reproduction and increased death.

exam.q: Explain why mutualistic relationships are often more stable than predator‑prey relationships.
model: In mutualism both species gain a benefit, so there is no direct conflict of interest; selection favours traits that maintain the interaction. In predator‑prey relationships each species has opposing goals – the predator wants to kill, the prey wants to survive – leading to continual arms races and potential collapse if one side is removed. Hence mutualisms tend to be more stable over time.
exam.tip: Contrast ‘both benefit’ with ‘one kills the other’; mention co‑evolutionary stability.

exam.q: A field experiment compares seed set in bagged (no pollinators) and open (pollinators free) flowers of a plant species. Predict the likely result and explain the relevance to mutualism.
model: Open flowers will produce significantly more seeds than bagged flowers because pollinators transfer pollen, increasing fertilisation. This demonstrates the mutualistic benefit to the plant (reproductive success) and to the pollinator (food).
exam.tip: State the expected quantitative difference (more seeds) and link to mutualism definition.

worked.q: In a predation experiment, 30 fruit flies are placed with 3 spiders for 2 hours. After the period 12 flies remain alive. Calculate the predation rate as a percentage.
steps: Number of flies eaten = initial – remaining = 30 – 12 = 18.
Predation rate = (flies eaten / initial flies) × 100 = (18/30) × 100 = 60 %.

worked.q: A plant species produces 200 seeds when pollinated by bees but only 40 seeds when pollinators are excluded. What is the percentage increase in seed set due to mutualism?
steps: Increase in seeds = 200 – 40 = 160.
Percentage increase = (160 / 40) × 100 = 400 %.

worked.q: During a parasitism study, infected fish grow at 0.8 cm per week while uninfected fish grow at 1.2 cm per week. What is the percentage reduction in growth caused by the parasite?
steps: Difference in growth = 1.2 – 0.8 = 0.4 cm/week.
Percentage reduction = (0.4 / 1.2) × 100 ≈ 33 %.

bio_ocra.10.4.summary: Abiotic and biotic factors shape the structure and dynamics of ecological communities. Abiotic factors such as temperature, light, water, pH and nutrients set the physical limits for species, while biotic factors like competition, predation, mutualism and parasitism determine how organisms interact and influence each other's survival and reproduction. Understanding these factors explains why certain species dominate particular habitats and how changes can lead to shifts in community composition.

core.h: Definition of Abiotic and Biotic Factors
core.p: Abiotic factors are the non‑living physical and chemical elements of an environment, whereas biotic factors are the living components and their interactions.
bullets: Abiotic: temperature, light intensity, water availability, pH, salinity, oxygen levels, soil type, nutrient concentrations.
Biotic: competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism, commensalism, disease.

callouts.p: A non‑living component of an ecosystem that influences the survival and distribution of organisms.
A living component of an ecosystem, including organisms themselves and the interactions between them.

core.h: Key Abiotic Factors and Their Effects
core.p: Each abiotic factor can limit or promote the presence of particular species, creating ecological niches.
bullets: **Temperature** – determines metabolic rates; extreme temperatures can denature enzymes.
**Light intensity** – controls photosynthetic rate; low light limits primary production.
**Water availability** – influences cell turgor, nutrient transport, and habitat type (aquatic vs terrestrial).
**pH** – affects enzyme activity and solubility of nutrients; most plants prefer pH 5.5‑7.0.
**Nutrient concentration** – nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium are essential for growth; deficiency limits biomass.

core.h: Key Biotic Factors and Their Effects
core.p: Biotic interactions determine how species coexist, compete for resources and affect each other's survival.
bullets: **Competition** – both intra‑ and interspecific; reduces resource availability, can lead to competitive exclusion.
**Predation** – predator consumes prey; controls prey population size and can drive evolutionary adaptations.
**Herbivory** – plant‑eating animals; influences plant community composition and biomass.
**Parasitism** – parasite benefits at host’s expense; can reduce host fitness and alter community dynamics.
**Mutualism** – both species benefit; often essential for nutrient acquisition (e.g., mycorrhizae).
**Commensalism** – one benefits, other unaffected; less impact on community structure.

callouts.p: Do not confuse *competition* with *predation* – competition is a struggle for the same resource, predation involves a consumer‑resource relationship.

core.h: How Abiotic Factors Influence Biotic Interactions
core.p: Abiotic conditions can modify the strength and outcome of biotic relationships.
bullets: Temperature affects predator metabolism – colder temps may reduce predation pressure.
Water stress can increase competition for moisture among plants.
pH can limit the distribution of mutualistic fungi, altering plant nutrient uptake.

callouts.p: The *environmental envelope* concept links abiotic limits to biotic interactions.

core.p: A niche describes the role and requirements of a species; the habitat is the physical environment.
bullets: Fundamental niche – range of conditions a species could occupy without competitors.
Realised niche – portion of the fundamental niche actually occupied, limited by biotic factors.
Habitat heterogeneity increases niche diversity, supporting richer communities.

callouts.p: The full range of environmental conditions under which a species can survive and reproduce.
The actual set of conditions a species occupies, constrained by biotic interactions such as competition.

core.p: During succession, abiotic conditions change, altering which biotic factors dominate.
bullets: Pioneer species modify soil pH and nutrient levels, allowing later species to establish.
Shade‑creating trees reduce light intensity, shifting competition from light to nutrients.
Decomposers increase soil organic matter, improving water retention.

callouts.p: When answering succession questions, always link the change in an abiotic factor to the subsequent biotic response.

core.h: Human Impacts on Abiotic and Biotic Factors
core.p: Anthropogenic activities modify both abiotic conditions and biotic interactions.
bullets: Pollution changes pH and nutrient levels, causing eutrophication.
Habitat fragmentation alters temperature and moisture regimes, increasing edge effects.
Introduced species add new biotic interactions (predation, competition).

core.p: Higher tier requires evaluation of how multiple abiotic and biotic factors interact to shape community dynamics.
bullets: Explain feedback loops – e.g., increased plant cover lowers temperature, which further promotes plant growth.
Discuss limiting factor principle – the factor in shortest supply controls community productivity.
Analyse case studies where a single abiotic change (e.g., acid rain) leads to cascading biotic effects.

callouts.p: Do not simply list factors; always link cause and effect and evaluate significance.

core.p: Typical OCR practical: effect of light intensity on algae growth.
bullets: Control variables: temperature, nutrient concentration, CO₂.
Independent variable: distance from light source (lux).
Dependent variable: increase in algal biomass (dry weight).
Result: growth rate rises with light up to a saturation point, then plateaus.

callouts.p: Always record the exact lux reading; it is the quantitative measure required by the mark scheme.

core.p: Understanding abiotic/biotic factors underpins the cycles of material, trophic structures and ecosystem stability.
bullets: Decomposers (B4.1d) are biotic factors that respond to temperature and moisture.
Trophic pyramids (B4.1i‑j) are shaped by the availability of abiotic resources.
Competition (B4.1g) is a biotic factor directly influenced by nutrient levels.

analogy.p: Think of an ecosystem like a theatre production. The stage lighting, temperature of the auditorium and acoustics are the abiotic factors – they set the conditions for the performance. The actors, director, stage crew and audience are the biotic factors – they interact, compete for spotlight, support each other, or sometimes sabotage the show. The analogy breaks down when you consider that in a theatre the lighting can be switched on or off at will, whereas abiotic factors in nature change more slowly and cannot be deliberately controlled.

terms.d: A non‑living physical or chemical component of an ecosystem that influences the organisms present.
A living component of an ecosystem, including organisms themselves and the interactions between them.
The full range of environmental conditions under which a species can survive and reproduce.
The portion of the fundamental niche actually occupied by a species because of biotic interactions.
An interaction where two or more organisms vie for the same limited resource.
A biological interaction where one organism (predator) kills and eats another (prey).
A symbiotic relationship where both species benefit.
A relationship where one organism benefits at the expense of the host.
The abiotic or biotic factor that is in shortest supply and therefore controls the rate of a process.
The range of abiotic conditions that a species can tolerate.
Changes in population or community structure that occur at the boundary of two habitats.
A process where the output of a system influences the input, either amplifying (positive) or dampening (negative) the original effect.

mistakes.w: Abiotic factors are only temperature and light.
mistakes.r: Abiotic factors include temperature, light, water, pH, nutrients, oxygen, salinity, etc.

mistakes.w: Competition and predation are the same because both involve two species.
mistakes.r: Competition is a struggle for the same resource; predation is a consumer‑resource interaction where one organism is killed.

mistakes.w: Realised niche is larger than the fundamental niche.
mistakes.r: The realised niche is always a subset of the fundamental niche because biotic interactions restrict it.

mistakes.w: All biotic interactions are beneficial.
mistakes.r: Biotic interactions can be beneficial (mutualism), neutral (commensalism) or harmful (predation, competition, parasitism).

mistakes.w: Increasing temperature always increases species richness.
mistakes.r: Temperature can increase metabolic rates but extreme temperatures can reduce species richness; the effect depends on tolerance ranges.

mistakes.w: pH does not affect nutrient availability.
mistakes.r: pH influences the solubility of many nutrients; extreme pH can make essential nutrients unavailable.

mistakes.w: Human impact only changes biotic factors.
mistakes.r: Human activities alter both abiotic (e.g., pollution, climate change) and biotic factors (e.g., species introductions).

exam.q: Define abiotic and biotic factors and give two examples of each that influence a pond community.
model: Abiotic factor – a non‑living component of an ecosystem (1). Example: temperature (1).
Biotic factor – a living component or interaction (1). Example: predation (1).
exam.tip: Use the exact terms ‘abiotic factor’ and ‘biotic factor’ – the mark scheme awards a point for each definition.

exam.q: Explain how a decrease in water availability would affect the competition between two plant species in a grassland.
model: Reduced water limits the amount each plant can uptake (1).
Both species now compete more intensely for the limited water (1).
The species with deeper roots or better drought tolerance will out‑compete the other (1).
Result: the less tolerant species may decline or be excluded (1).
Link to limiting factor principle – water becomes the limiting factor (1).
Overall community composition shifts towards drought‑tolerant species (1).
exam.tip: Structure answer: effect → interaction → outcome → link to principle.

exam.q: A woodland is being cleared and replaced by a field. List three abiotic changes that are likely to occur and explain how each could influence the biotic community.
model: Increase in light intensity (1) – favours sun‑loving plants, reduces shade‑tolerant species (1).
Increase in temperature (1) – raises metabolic rates, may allow thermophilic insects to colonise (1).
Decrease in soil moisture (1) – reduces water‑dependent species, promotes drought‑tolerant grasses (1).
Each abiotic change alters the niche conditions, causing a shift in species composition (4).
exam.tip: Give a clear cause‑effect link for each abiotic change.

exam.q: Discuss how mutualistic relationships can help a plant species survive in nutrient‑poor soil.
model: Mycorrhizal fungi increase surface area for nutrient absorption (1).
Fungi obtain carbohydrates from the plant (1).
Result: plant gains more nitrogen/phosphorus, improving growth in poor soil (1).
Mutualism therefore expands the plant’s realised niche (1).
Provides a competitive advantage over plants without such partners (1).
Overall community may have higher plant diversity due to niche differentiation (1).
exam.tip: Mention both sides of the relationship and link to niche concepts.

exam.q: Why might a species that is a strong competitor in one habitat be a weak competitor in another? Use examples.
model: Competitiveness depends on abiotic conditions (1).
Example: a shade‑tolerant fern outcompetes others in low light but is outcompeted by grasses in full sun (1).
Thus, the same species can be strong or weak depending on the abiotic envelope (2).
exam.tip: Use a concrete example and tie back to abiotic factors.

exam.q: Explain how an increase in temperature could lead to a change in predator‑prey dynamics in a marine ecosystem.
model: Higher temperature raises metabolic rates of both predator and prey (1).
Prey may grow faster, increasing their numbers (1).
Predators may need to eat more to meet energy demands (1).
If prey increase faster than predator consumption, prey population may rise (1).
Alternatively, if predator cannot keep up, prey may escape predation pressure (1).
Result: shift in population sizes and possible trophic cascade (1).
exam.tip: Show the chain of cause‑effect and consider both possible outcomes.

exam.q: A lake has become eutrophic after fertilizer runoff. Identify the abiotic factor responsible and describe two biotic consequences.
model: Abiotic factor: excess nitrogen/phosphorus (1).
Biotic consequence 1: algal bloom – rapid algae growth (1).
Biotic consequence 2: oxygen depletion – death of fish and other aerobic organisms (1).
Additional consequence: shift to dominance of tolerant species (1).
Link to decomposition and oxygen consumption (1).
exam.tip: Link the abiotic cause directly to the biotic effects.

exam.q: Evaluate how edge effects can modify both abiotic and biotic factors in a fragmented forest.
model: Edge receives more sunlight → higher temperature and lower humidity (abiotic) (1).
Wind penetration changes soil moisture (abiotic) (1).
These changes favour light‑loving, drought‑tolerant species (biotic) (1).
Increased predator access leads to higher predation rates (biotic) (1).
Overall biodiversity may decline due to loss of interior‑specialist species (1).
However, some edge‑adapted species may increase, raising overall species count (1).
Evaluation: benefits for some species, overall negative for specialist interior species (1).
Conclusion: edge effects alter both abiotic conditions and biotic interactions, reshaping community composition (1).
exam.tip: Balance positive and negative impacts in your evaluation.

worked.q: In a controlled experiment, algae are grown under three light intensities: 500 lux, 1000 lux and 1500 lux. Biomass (dry weight) after 7 days is 12 mg, 25 mg and 30 mg respectively. Explain the trend using the concept of a limiting factor.
steps: Identify light as the variable being changed.
Observe that biomass increases as light intensity rises, showing a positive relationship.
Note that the increase from 1000 to 1500 lux is smaller than from 500 to 1000 lux, indicating a plateau.
Apply the limiting factor principle: at low light, light limits photosynthesis; as light increases, the limitation shifts to another factor (e.g., nutrients).
Conclude that light is the limiting factor up to ~1000 lux; beyond this, another factor becomes limiting, so growth rate slows.
worked.ans: Light limits photosynthetic rate at low intensities; as light increases, growth rises until another factor (e.g., nutrients) becomes limiting, causing the plateau.

worked.q: A pond’s pH drops from 7.5 to 5.5 due to acid rain. Predict two effects on the biotic community and justify them.
steps: Recognise that many freshwater organisms have optimal pH around neutral.
Lower pH can reduce calcium carbonate availability, affecting shell‑forming organisms.
Acid‑sensitive species (e.g., many fish and amphibian larvae) may experience reduced survival.
Acid‑tolerant species (e.g., certain algae and mosses) may increase, altering competition.
worked.ans: 1) Decline of calcium‑dependent organisms (e.g., snail shells dissolve). 2) Increase in acid‑tolerant algae, shifting competitive balance.

bio_ocra.10.6.summary: Trophic levels describe the feeding positions of organisms within an ecosystem, tracking how energy and biomass flow from primary sources to top predators. Producers sit at the base, creating their own food via photosynthesis, while primary, secondary, and tertiary consumers feed sequentially along food chains and food webs. Understanding these levels allows us to analyse feeding relationships, ecosystem stability, and the fundamental structure of biological communities.

core.p: Trophic levels are the hierarchical feeding positions within an ecological food chain or food web. Each level represents a specific step in the flow of energy and the cycling of matter through an ecosystem.
bullets: Organisms are grouped by how they obtain their food and energy.
The word 'trophic' comes from the Greek word 'trophos', meaning nourishment or feeding.
Energy always flows in a single direction through trophic levels, starting from a light source.
At each step up a trophic level, a significant amount of energy is lost as heat through respiration.

callouts.p: The position of an organism in a food chain, food web, or ecological pyramid, determined by its feeding relationships.
Energy enters ecosystems via sunlight and moves upwards through trophic levels, but cannot be recycled back down.

core.p: Producers form the essential first trophic level of every food chain. They are autotrophs that manufacture their own organic molecules and biomass using light energy from the sun.
bullets: Green plants and algae use chlorophyll to absorb light energy during photosynthesis.
They convert inorganic substances (carbon dioxide and water) into organic compounds like glucose.
Chemoautotrophic bacteria also act as producers in extreme environments like deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
Producers do not depend on other living organisms for nutrition, making them the foundation of ecosystems.

callouts.p: An organism that makes its own food using sunlight or chemical energy, occupying the first trophic level.

core.p: Primary consumers occupy the second trophic level and are organisms that feed directly upon producers. They are heterotrophs that gain their nutrients by consuming plant or algal matter.
bullets: Commonly referred to as herbivores because they eat plants exclusively.
Examples include rabbits, caterpillars, cows, zooplankton, and koalas.
They digest plant cell walls (cellulose) using specialized gut bacteria or enzymes.
They convert plant biomass into animal biomass, though much is respired or lost as waste.

callouts.p: Primary consumers must eat large volumes of plant material because plant matter has a lower energy density per unit weight than animal tissue.

core.p: Secondary consumers occupy the third trophic level and are carnivores or omnivores that feed upon primary consumers.
bullets: They obtain their energy by hunting or scavenging primary consumers (herbivores).
Examples include frogs eating grasshoppers, small birds eating caterpillars, and spiders eating flies.
Omnivores like humans and bears can act as secondary consumers when eating herbivorous animals.
They generally possess specialized predatory adaptations such as sharp teeth, claws, or venom.

callouts.p: A carnivore or omnivore that eats primary consumers, occupying the third trophic level.

core.h: Trophic Level 4 and Above: Tertiary and Apex Consumers
core.p: Higher trophic levels consist of tertiary consumers, which eat secondary consumers, and apex predators at the absolute peak of the food chain.
bullets: Tertiary consumers include large carnivores like hawks, killer whales, and large fish.
Apex predators have no natural predators of their own within their adult ecosystem.
Examples of apex predators include lions, polar bears, great white sharks, and golden eagles.
Food chains rarely extend beyond four or five trophic levels due to the cumulative loss of energy.

callouts.p: Be careful: an animal's trophic level can change depending on what it eats in a specific food web. Omnivores can occupy multiple trophic levels simultaneously.

core.p: A food chain is a simplified linear model that shows the direct transfer of food energy from one specific organism to the next.
bullets: Always starts with a producer and ends with a top carnivore.
Arrows within food chains point in the direction of energy flow (from the organism eaten to the organism eating it).
Example: Grass -> Rabbit -> Fox -> Flea (parasite).
Useful for calculations and simple tracking, but unrealistic because most organisms eat multiple food types.

callouts.p: Never draw arrows pointing from the predator to the prey. The arrow means 'is eaten by' or shows the direction of biomass transfer.

core.p: A food web consists of many overlapping, interconnected food chains within a single habitat, representing real-world ecological complexity.
bullets: Reflects the reality that most animals have varied diets and are eaten by multiple predators.
Provides ecosystem resilience: if one prey species declines, predators can switch to alternative food sources.
Removal or population crash of a single keystone species can destabilize the entire web.
Arrows still represent the direction of energy and biomass transfer between interacting populations.

callouts.p: Complex food webs with high biodiversity are generally more stable than simple food chains when faced with environmental changes.

core.p: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) and detritivores (woodlice, earthworms) break down dead organic matter and waste products across all trophic levels.
bullets: They secrete extracellular enzymes onto dead material and absorb the digested breakdown products.
Although often omitted from standard linear food chain diagrams, they process waste from every trophic level.
They recycle vital inorganic nutrients (like nitrates and phosphates) back into the soil for producers.
Without decomposers, nutrients would remain locked in dead bodies and producers would run out of raw materials.

callouts.p: An organism, chiefly bacteria or fungi, that breaks down dead organic matter using extracellular digestion.

core.p: Organisms are fundamentally categorized based on how they synthesize or acquire organic carbon compounds.
bullets: Autotrophs make their own organic food from simple inorganic raw materials (producers).
Heterotrophs must ingest or absorb pre-formed organic molecules from other living or dead organisms (consumers and decomposers).
All animals, fungi, and many bacteria are heterotrophic.
Plants, algae, and some bacteria are autotrophic.

callouts.p: An organism that cannot manufacture its own food and must obtain organic carbon by consuming other organisms.

core.h: The Role of Omnivores in Trophic Levels
core.p: Omnivores consume both plant and animal matter, meaning they can occupy multiple trophic levels simultaneously depending on their meal.
bullets: When a human eats an apple, they act as a primary consumer (Trophic Level 2).
When that same human eats a beef steak (from a cow that ate grass), they act as a secondary or tertiary consumer.
This flexibility complicates the drawing of simple food webs.
It also allows omnivores to survive food shortages by switching between trophic levels.

callouts.p: If an exam question asks for the trophic level of an omnivore, check the specific food chain provided in the stem rather than assuming a fixed level.

core.p: Persistent toxic chemicals (such as heavy metals or pesticides like DDT) can accumulate and magnify in concentration as they pass up trophic levels.
bullets: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a substance within an individual organism over its lifespan.
Biomagnification is the multiplying concentration of a toxin in tissues at successively higher trophic levels.
Apex predators end up with dangerously high concentrations of toxins because they ingest the accumulated load of many prey items.
Explains why apex predators like eagles and polar bears suffer most from environmental pollution.

callouts.p: Toxin concentration increases exponentially at higher trophic levels because animals eat large quantities of lower-level organisms to gain energy.

analogy.t: The Multi-Storey Restaurant and Supply Chain
analogy.p:
Imagine a giant multi-storey restaurant. The ground floor is a massive kitchen (Producers) that grows its own ingredients from sunlight and water. The second floor (Primary Consumers) consists of customers who buy and eat raw vegetables. The third floor (Secondary Consumers) consists of chefs who eat the vegetable-eaters, and the penthouse (Apex Predators) hosts guests who eat everyone below them. Each floor up requires food to be transported, and at every single flight of stairs, food gets dropped, eaten by mice, or wasted, meaning there are fewer meals left for the top floor.

Where it breaks down: In a restaurant, food is brought in from the outside world, whereas an ecosystem's energy must originate exclusively from incoming sunlight, and matter is fully recycled by decomposers rather than thrown into a municipal bin.

terms.d: The position of an organism in a food chain or food web, categorized by its feeding relationship.
An autotrophic organism, usually a green plant or alga, that synthesizes organic molecules using light energy.
A herbivore that feeds directly on producers, occupying the second trophic level.
A carnivore or omnivore that feeds on primary consumers, occupying the third trophic level.
A carnivore that feeds on secondary consumers, occupying the fourth trophic level.
A top-level carnivore with no natural predators in its ecosystem.
A linear diagram showing the transfer of energy and biomass from one organism to the next.
A network of interlocking and intersecting food chains in a biological community.
An organism that produces its own complex organic food from simple inorganic substances.
An organism that obtains carbon and energy by consuming other living or dead organisms.
Bacteria or fungi that break down dead material via extracellular digestion.
An animal that feeds on dead organic debris, breaking it down into smaller pieces.
The increasing concentration of toxic substances in organism tissues at successively higher trophic levels.
An animal anatomically adapted to feed exclusively on plants.
An animal that feeds on other animals.

mistakes.w: Saying that arrows in a food chain show who eats whom.
mistakes.r: Arrows show the direction of energy and biomass transfer (meaning 'is eaten by' or 'energy passes to').

mistakes.w: Placing decomposers at the top of a food chain.
mistakes.r: Decomposers process dead matter and waste from all trophic levels, not just the top level.

mistakes.w: Stating that primary consumers are always carnivores.
mistakes.r: Primary consumers are always herbivores because they feed directly on producers.

mistakes.w: Believing energy can cycle endlessly through trophic levels.
mistakes.r: Energy flows in one direction and is eventually lost entirely as heat; only matter is recycled.

mistakes.w: Assuming an animal always belongs to the same trophic level.
mistakes.r: Omnivores change their trophic level depending on whether they eat plants or animals in a given food web.

mistakes.w: Calling the sun a trophic level.
mistakes.r: The sun is the external source of light energy, not a trophic level itself (producers are level 1).

mistakes.w: Writing that apex predators create energy.
mistakes.r: All organisms only transform or transfer energy; producers capture it from sunlight, and consumers transfer it.

exam.q: Define the term 'trophic level'.
model: The position of an organism in a food chain, food web, or ecological pyramid.
exam.tip: Keep definitions concise and precise; do not waffle about energy loss here.

exam.q: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
model: Energy is lost at each trophic level (due to respiration, excretion, and uneaten parts).
Insufficient energy remains at higher levels to support a viable population of top predators.
exam.tip: Mention both energy loss and the consequence (not enough energy left for another level).

exam.q: Look at the food chain: Grass -> Rabbit -> Fox. State the trophic level of the fox.
model: Trophic level 3 (secondary consumer).
exam.tip: Count carefully: Grass is level 1, Rabbit is level 2, Fox is level 3.

exam.q: Describe the difference between an autotroph and a heterotroph.
model: Autotrophs make their own organic food using sunlight or chemicals (producers).
Heterotrophs must consume other organisms to obtain organic nutrients.
exam.tip: Use comparative language to ensure both terms are clearly defined.

exam.q: Explain the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
model: Break down dead organic matter and waste products.
Secrete enzymes to digest material externally and absorb nutrients.
Release inorganic nutrients back into the soil for producers to reuse.
exam.tip: Always mention nutrient recycling for full marks.

exam.q: Draw or describe the direction of arrows in a food web diagram and explain why they point that way.
model: Arrows point from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it.
This shows the direction in which energy and biomass are transferred.
exam.tip: Never get the arrow direction backwards; remember it points in the direction energy travels.

exam.q: Explain how biomagnification affects apex predators differently than primary consumers.
model: Toxic chemicals are not broken down or excreted easily by organisms.
As animals eat many lower-trophic-level organisms, toxins accumulate in their fatty tissues.
Apex predators ingest the accumulated load of numerous prey items, resulting in the highest concentrations.
exam.tip: Link the number of organisms eaten to the multiplication of toxin concentration.

exam.q: Give two reasons why primary consumers do not convert 100% of the plant biomass they eat into their own body biomass.
model: Energy is lost through respiration as heat.
Energy/biomass is lost in waste products (faeces and urine) or uneaten plant parts (roots, bark).
exam.tip: Learn standard loss pathways: respiration, excretion, egestion, and uneaten parts.

exam.q: An omnivore eats berries and mice. Explain how its trophic level changes between these two meals.
model: When eating berries, the omnivore acts as a primary consumer (trophic level 2).
When eating mice (which eat plants), the omnivore acts as a secondary consumer (trophic level 3).
exam.tip: State both meals and explicitly link each to its corresponding trophic level number.

worked.q: A food chain is: Algae -> Zooplankton -> Small Fish -> Salmon -> Osprey. Identify the primary consumer and the tertiary consumer in this food chain.
steps: Step 1: Identify trophic level 1 (the producer). Algae is the producer.
Step 2: Identify trophic level 2 (the primary consumer, eating the producer). Zooplankton is the primary consumer.
Step 3: Count up to trophic level 4 to find the tertiary consumer. Algae (1), Zooplankton (2), Small Fish (3), Salmon (4). Salmon is the tertiary consumer.
worked.ans: Primary consumer: Zooplankton. Tertiary consumer: Salmon.

worked.q: Explain why a farmer producing crops for humans to eat directly (Trophic Level 1 to Level 2) is more energy-efficient than feeding those crops to cattle and then eating the beef (Trophic Level 1 to Level 2 to Level 3).
steps: Step 1: Note that energy is lost at each trophic level transition (roughly 90% lost, 10% transferred).
Step 2: Eating crops directly involves only one energy transfer step from the sun/producer.
Step 3: Eating beef involves an extra trophic level, meaning two major energy loss steps occur.
Step 4: Conclude that more people can be fed per hectare of land with a plant-based diet because less energy is wasted through animal respiration and waste.
worked.ans: Direct plant consumption avoids the energy losses associated with an extra trophic level, leaving vastly more usable food energy available for humans.
